title: Sealants on Threaded Plumbing Connections: Tape, Dope, and Wicking
summary: This Old House presents a viewer Q&A on sealing threaded plumbing connections. The host contrasts tapered (plumbing) threads with common straight threads, then demonstrates several sealing options: teflon tape (PTFE tape) application, non-hardening pipe thread sealant (pipe dope), and the wick method for older work. The discussion covers when to apply each method, how to apply around threads, and situational choices such as using rubber gaskets or relying on a ground joint instead of thread sealants for certain connections like radiators and faucets. The result is a practical guide to selecting and applying sealants or gaskets to achieve a removable, leak-free seal without over-sealing.
topics: when not to use thread sealant on straight threads

sections.title: Intro: Tapered versus straight threads in plumbing
concepts: machine vs tapered thread
plumbing uses tapered thread
shape change along the thread as it tightens
visual example of a tapered thread on pipe
sections.description: Richard explains that most threaded plumbing uses a tapered thread, not the straight thread seen on nuts and bolts. He demonstrates how a pipe’s threads vary in diameter along their length, causing tighter engagement as the thread travels, and notes that a straight-thread connection does not self-tighten in the same way. This sets the context for why sealing is needed even when the threads appear to thread together.

sections.title: Teflon tape: application and wrapping technique
concepts: Teflon tape as popular thread sealant
wrapping technique to seal on itself
tape tension to fill threads
sections.description: The host introduces teflon tape as the modern standard for many threaded connections. He demonstrates holding the work in the left hand, wrapping the tape around the threads with tension so it binds to itself, and building several tight layers before threading the fitting together to form a seal.

sections.title: Pipe dope: liquid thread sealant and its properties
concepts: pipe dope as an alternative to teflon tape
fill between threads without hardening
removability of the connection
sections.description: The video shows pipe sealant (pipe dope) as another common option. It is described as a liquid that fills the gaps between threads but does not harden, preserving the ability to disassemble the joint later. The host notes a preference for this approach in some cases, while emphasizing removability.

sections.title: Wicking (sealant wick) for old-work connections
concepts: wicking as a way to seal older threads
inserting wick into the thread to carry sealant
expansion of wick when liquid contact occurs
sections.description: For connections involving old work, the host demonstrates using a thread-wicking material. A single strand is pulled and laid into the threads so that, when liquid sealant is applied, the wick expands slightly and helps create a seal. This illustrates a clever method for retrofitting seals on legacy joints.

sections.title: When not to seal every threaded joint: straight vs ground joints
concepts: not all threaded joints require sealant
ground joint concept
face-to-face tightening provides a liquid-tight seal
sections.description: The host explains that some connections use straight threads that are drawn together by the mating faces, forming a ground joint rather than relying on thread sealant alone. He demonstrates that in certain cases, a thread sealant might not be needed or used in moderation, and emphasizes proper tightening against the mating surface.

sections.title: Faucet and valve connections with rubber gaskets
concepts: rubber gaskets present on some new fittings
no thread sealant on gasketed joints
tighten to compress the gasket
sections.description: The video points out that some newer faucet connections already include rubber gaskets. In these cases, no thread sealant is required; simply tighten enough to compress the gasket to achieve a seal.

sections.title: Conclusion: practical guidance on seals
concepts: choose the appropriate sealing method
consider joint type and accessibility
prioritize removability
sections.description: In closing, the host reiterates that the right sealing method depends on the joint type (tapered vs straight, gasketed vs non-gasketed) and the need for future disassembly. The guidance emphasizes practicality and serviceability.
